auckland: Auckland, known as the City of Sails, welcomed us with its vibrant harbor and cosmopolitan atmosphere. We spent the day exploring the bustling city center, sampling incredible cuisine from around the world, and soaking in the views of the Waitemata Harbour. The mix of urban sophistication and natural beauty gave us a perfect introduction to New Zealand.
auckland-harbour: The Auckland Harbour is the gateway to adventure. From the historic ferry buildings, we caught our first glimpse of the islands dotting the Hauraki Gulf. The harbor buzzes with activity — ferries, yachts, and fishing boats creating a constant maritime dance.
waiheke: Waiheke Island exceeded all expectations. Just 40 minutes by ferry from Auckland, this paradise island offers world-class wineries, stunning beaches, and a relaxed Mediterranean vibe. The turquoise waters and golden sand beaches made us forget we were in the South Pacific.
waiheke-bike: Exploring Waiheke by eBike was pure joy. We cruised through rolling vineyards, stopped at boutique wineries for tastings, and discovered hidden beaches along the coast. The gentle hills were no match for our electric steeds, letting us cover the island's highlights without breaking a sweat.
queenstown: Queenstown lived up to its reputation as the adventure capital of New Zealand. Surrounded by the dramatic Remarkables mountain range and nestled on the shores of Lake Wakatipu, this town pulses with energy. Picking up our campervan here marked the true beginning of our South Island adventure.
crown-range: The Crown Range Road is one of New Zealand's most spectacular alpine drives. Climbing to 1,076 meters, the highest sealed road in the country, we were treated to jaw-dropping views of the mountains and valleys below. Every hairpin turn revealed a new panorama more stunning than the last.
wanaka: Wanaka captured our hearts with its laid-back charm. This lakeside town, smaller and quieter than Queenstown, offers the same stunning mountain backdrop but with a more relaxed vibe. The famous Wanaka Tree, standing alone in the lake, has become an icon of New Zealand's natural beauty.
roys-peak: The climb to Roys Peak was challenging but incredibly rewarding. After hours of steady ascent through tussock-covered slopes, we reached the summit and were greeted by one of the most iconic views in New Zealand — Lake Wanaka stretching below, surrounded by snow-capped peaks reaching toward the clouds.
red-bridge-camp: Red Bridge campground offered a peaceful retreat near Lake Hawea. Waking up to the sound of birds and the sight of mist rising from the lake was magical. This DOC campsite perfectly embodies the simple beauty of camping in New Zealand's backcountry.
queenstown-paknsave: A practical pit stop, but an essential one. Stocking up on supplies for the road ahead, we filled our campervan with local produce, snacks, and everything needed for self-sufficient travel through the remote Fiordland region.
te-anau: Te Anau is the gateway to Fiordland, New Zealand's largest national park. This peaceful lakeside town sits on the edge of wilderness, where mountains plunge into deep fiords. The tranquil atmosphere belied the adventure that awaited us in the coming days.
lake-marian: Lake Marian is a hidden gem in the heart of Fiordland. The track winds through ancient beech forest before opening up to reveal a pristine alpine lake, its surface a perfect mirror reflecting the surrounding peaks. The stillness here was almost sacred.
lake-gunn: Walking through Lake Gunn's ancient beech forest felt like stepping back in time. The moss-draped trees and crystal-clear water of the lake created an otherworldly atmosphere. This short walk offered a glimpse into New Zealand's primeval forests.
cascade-creek: Cascade Creek campsite became our base for exploring Fiordland. Surrounded by towering peaks and lush rainforest, falling asleep to the sound of rushing water was the perfect end to our adventure-filled days.
milford-sound: Milford Sound — Piopiotahi in Maori — is often called the eighth wonder of the world, and we understood why. Sheer cliffs rise 1,200 meters from the dark waters, waterfalls cascade down the rock faces, and seals bask on the rocks. Our cruise took us past Mitre Peak and out toward the Tasman Sea.
gertrude-saddle: The Gertrude Saddle track is not for the faint-hearted. This challenging climb through alpine terrain rewards the brave with breathtaking views of the Darran Mountains and beyond. Standing at the saddle, with the world falling away on all sides, we felt truly on top of the world.
queenstown-small-planet: Small Planet in Queenstown equipped us with everything needed for our backcountry camping adventure. Tents, sleeping bags, cooking gear — everything essential for a night under the stars near a glacier.
earnslaw-burn-parking: The Earnslaw Burn trailhead marks the beginning of one of New Zealand's hidden treasures. Parking among the beech trees, we prepared for our trek into a valley few visitors ever see.
earnslaw-burn: Camping beneath the Earnslaw Glacier was an experience we'll never forget. The valley, carved by ancient ice, led us to a spot where we could watch the glacier's blue ice catching the last light of day. Sleeping in our tent with this view was surreal.
queenstown-camp: Back in Queenstown after our backcountry adventure, we appreciated the simple comforts of a proper campsite. Hot showers never felt so good after days in the wilderness.
arrowtown: Spending Christmas Eve in Arrowtown was magical. This historic gold-mining village, with its preserved heritage buildings and tree-lined streets, felt like stepping into a storybook. The festive atmosphere and warm summer evening made for a uniquely New Zealand Christmas.
lake-tekapo: Lake Tekapo's impossibly turquoise waters are fed by glacial flour from the nearby mountains. We spent hours walking along the shores, marveling at the color that seems too vivid to be real. The Church of the Good Shepherd provided a perfect frame for this natural masterpiece.
mackenzie-rv-camp: Our campsite in the Mackenzie Basin offered front-row seats to some of the darkest skies in the world. This area is designated as an International Dark Sky Reserve, and the stars that night lived up to the promise.
tekapo-spa: Soaking in the Tekapo hot pools with views of the turquoise lake and snow-capped mountains was pure bliss. The contrast of warm water and cool mountain air, combined with that incredible view, created a moment of perfect relaxation.
lake-pukaki: Lake Pukaki's brilliant blue waters stretch toward Aoraki/Mount Cook, creating one of New Zealand's most photographed scenes. We spent time at viewpoints along the shore, watching the light play on the lake and mountains throughout the day.
mt-cook: Aoraki/Mount Cook, at 3,724 meters, is New Zealand's highest peak. The village at its base provided our launching point for exploring the surrounding trails and glaciers. The scale of these mountains is humbling.
sealy-tarns: The climb to Sealy Tarns was steep but rewarding. These small alpine lakes, reflecting the massive face of Mount Cook, offered a spectacular vantage point. The famous Mueller Hut sits above, for those seeking an even higher adventure.
blue-lakes: The Blue Lakes walk revealed turquoise pools formed by glacial melt, with the massive Tasman Glacier looming behind. This easy trail through tussock and scrub showcased the dramatic landscape shaped by thousands of years of ice.
chamberlains-ford: Chamberlains Ford was our quiet freedom camping spot for the night. Tucked away from the main roads, we had the place almost to ourselves, enjoying the simple pleasure of a peaceful evening in the New Zealand countryside.
christchurch: Christchurch, the Garden City, is a place of resilience and renewal. Still rebuilding after the 2011 earthquake, the city has transformed itself with innovative architecture, street art, and a vibrant culture that refuses to be defined by tragedy.
akaroa: Akaroa's French heritage gives this harbor town a unique charm. The historic buildings, French street names, and excellent cuisine reflect the town's history as an early French settlement. The harbor, formed in an ancient volcanic crater, is home to dolphins and penguins.
akaroa-kayaking: Kayaking in Akaroa harbor brought us close to nature in the most peaceful way. Paddling through the calm waters, we spotted Hector's dolphins — the world's smallest and rarest — playing in our wake. The volcanic cliffs towering above completed the magical experience.
bealey-spur: The Bealey Spur track took us through some of the most beautiful beech forest in New Zealand. As we climbed, the views opened up to reveal the snow-capped peaks of the Southern Alps stretching to the horizon.
devils-punch-bowl: The Devil's Punchbowl waterfall cascades 131 meters down a narrow chasm. The short walk to the viewing platform built up anticipation, then the falls burst into view — a powerful column of water surrounded by lush rainforest.
jacksons: Jackson's Retreat provided a cozy base on the West Coast. This family-run holiday park, nestled in the mountains, offered warm hospitality and a chance to dry out after exploring the notoriously wet West Coast.
franz-josef: Franz Josef town serves as the gateway to one of the world's most accessible glaciers. We spent the evening exploring the small town's excellent restaurants and bars, preparing for our glacier adventure the next day.
orange-sheep: Our accommodation in Franz Josef gave us a comfortable base for exploring the glacier region. The quirky name matched the relaxed West Coast vibe we'd come to love.
alex-knob: The Alex Knob track challenged us with its relentless climb, but the summit views made every step worthwhile. From the top, we could see the Franz Josef Glacier, the Tasman Sea, and the Southern Alps all in one incredible panorama.
brewster-trailhead: Camping at the Brewster trailhead, we prepared for one of the South Island's great alpine adventures. The evening light on the mountains promised good weather for our climb.
brewster-hut: The Brewster Track delivered an alpine experience beyond our expectations. Climbing through forest and alpine meadows, we reached views of glaciers and peaks that seemed to go on forever. The reward matched the effort.
blue-pools: Blue Pools was the perfect stop after our hike. A short track led us through moss-covered beech forest to a swing bridge over crystal-clear pools. The turquoise and emerald water was so transparent we could see every rock on the bottom. The stunning color comes from glacial flour washed down from the upper Haast River. Visitors are warned against swimming in the cold water, but the view from the bridge was reward enough.
red-bridge-camp-return: Returning to Red Bridge felt like coming home. The familiar campsite welcomed us back, and we reflected on the incredible journey through the glaciers and mountains of the West Coast.
wanaka-center: Our rest day in Wanaka's center was well-earned. Exploring the town's cafes, shops, and lakefront, we recharged for the adventures still to come. The Wanaka Tree was even more beautiful than we'd imagined.
hampshire-wanaka: Hampshire Holiday Parks in Wanaka gave us a comfortable night's rest. After weeks of camping, the facilities felt luxurious, and we made the most of the hot showers and kitchen facilities.
queenstown-explore: Exploring Queenstown without the rush of our first visit revealed a different side of this adventure town. We discovered hidden cafes, walked along the lake, and soaked in the atmosphere of this remarkable place.
black-sheep: Black Sheep Backpackers in Queenstown provided a social base for our last night in the South Island. The hostel's atmosphere was perfect for meeting fellow travelers and swapping stories of our adventures.
wellington: Wellington welcomed us with its characteristic wind and creative spirit. We explored Cuba Street's cafes and boutiques, rode the famous Cable Car, and wandered through the beautiful Botanic Garden overlooking the harbor.
porirua: Our Airbnb in Porirua gave us a local's perspective on life in the Wellington region. Away from the tourist areas, we experienced the everyday New Zealand that most visitors miss.
powell-hut-trailhead: The Tararua Ranges loom over Wellington, and the Powell Hut track offered our chance to explore these often-underrated mountains. The trailhead marked the start of a challenging but rewarding day.
powell-hut: The climb to Powell Hut pushed us to our limits, but the ridge views were worth every step. The Tararuas may be smaller than the Southern Alps, but they're equally wild and beautiful.
hastings: Hastings sits at the heart of Hawke's Bay wine country. The town's Art Deco architecture, a result of rebuilding after the 1931 earthquake, gives it a unique character. We explored the wineries and orchards that make this region famous.
hastings-golf: A morning round of golf in Hastings was a perfect way to experience the region's beautiful countryside. The well-maintained course offered views of vineyards and mountains between shots.
hastings-wine: Touring the wineries of Hawke's Bay was a highlight of our North Island journey. This region produces some of New Zealand's finest wines, and we enjoyed sampling Chardonnays and Syrahs at cellar doors throughout the day.
waimarama: The waves at Waimarama Beach were calling, and we answered. This beautiful stretch of sand on the Hawke's Bay coast provided perfect conditions for a morning surf. The uncrowded lineup was a pleasant surprise.
napier: Napier's Art Deco architecture makes it unique in New Zealand. Rebuilt after the devastating 1931 earthquake, the city center is a living museum of 1930s design. Our lunch stop turned into hours of exploration.
taupo: Taupo sits on the shores of New Zealand's largest lake. The town is a hub for adventure activities, but we appreciated its more relaxed side — walking along the lakefront and watching the sunset over the mountains.
spa-park: Spa Park's hot springs offered a unique experience — soaking in naturally heated water while the cold Waikato River rushed by. Finding the perfect temperature meant moving between the hot stream and the cool river.
turangi: Turangi served as our base for the Tongariro crossing. This small town lives for the mountains, and the anticipation of the next day's adventure was palpable among the hikers filling the cafes and hostels.
tongariro-start: The Mangatepopo car park at dawn was buzzing with excitement. Hikers from around the world prepared for what many call New Zealand's greatest day walk, and we were among them.
tongariro: The Tongariro Alpine Crossing lived up to its legendary status. Walking past volcanic craters, emerald lakes, and steaming vents, we felt like we were on another planet. The views from Red Crater and the descent past the Blue Lake will stay with us forever.
rotorua: Rotorua's geothermal activity makes it unlike anywhere else in New Zealand. The sulfur smell, steaming pools, and bubbling mud pots create a landscape that feels prehistoric. The Maori culture here is strong and welcoming.
kaituna-cascades: White water rafting on the Kaituna River was an adrenaline rush like no other. The highlight — plunging over the 7-meter Tutea Falls — was both terrifying and exhilarating. We emerged soaked but grinning.
mt-maunganui: Mount Maunganui's base track offered stunning coastal views with each step. The beach below stretched in a perfect arc, and surfers dotted the waves. This short hike was the perfect way to stretch our legs.
tairua: Tairua on the Coromandel Peninsula was our base for exploring this stunning coastline. The laid-back beach town atmosphere was a welcome change of pace as we prepared for our final adventures.
pinnacles-trailhead: The Pinnacles trailhead marked the start of our last major hike in New Zealand. The forest here is special — kauri trees tower overhead, survivors of a time when dinosaurs roamed.
pinnacles: The Pinnacles track led us through stunning native forest to views across the entire Coromandel Peninsula. Standing at the summit, looking out over the ocean on both sides, we felt the full majesty of New Zealand's natural beauty.
sailors-grave: Sailors Grave beach was our last taste of New Zealand paradise. This secluded stretch of sand near Tairua was the perfect place to reflect on our incredible journey. We lingered as long as possible before heading to the airport.
auckland-airport: Returning our rental car at Auckland Airport marked the end of our adventure. 27 days, countless memories, and a deep love for this beautiful country. New Zealand had captured our hearts.
home: Back home, but forever changed. The memories of New Zealand's mountains, beaches, and people will stay with us always. What a trip this has been — an adventure of a lifetime across Aotearoa.
